cim: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy
cim_eredeti: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy
szoveg_eredeti:
Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy

Integrating generative artificial intelligence into digital textile design substantially reduces perceived operational workload and accelerates procedural task completion, but it simultaneously weakens creative autonomy, personal style articulation, and overall design satisfaction. In a controlled investigation published in the journal Fashion and Textiles, researcher Shin Young Jang examined how algorithmic text-to-vector workflows reshape the cognitive demands and expressive agency of design students. Thirty-four third-year undergraduate fashion design students completed matched textile pattern design tasks using both traditional vector software and automated generative tools. The paired experimental comparisons demonstrated that while generative algorithms simplified technical execution, they also introduced distinct cognitive and creative trade-offs, shifting the human role from hands-on visual construction to selective curation.

The study was situated within an ongoing debate regarding how automated systems influence human-computer interaction, cognitive engagement, and creative authorship. As generative features become standard components of professional creative software suites, such as Adobe Illustrator and Photoshop through Firefly integrations, algorithmic models can autonomously generate visual assets from brief text prompts. While these tools lower barrier entry points and eliminate repetitive manual rendering, scholars have raised concerns over potential cognitive offloading, diminished agency, and reduced reflective problem-solving during foundational design learning. To systematically measure these phenomena in digital textile design, the investigation applied Cognitive Load Theory alongside the Creativity Support Index framework to evaluate both the cognitive effort expended during the design process and the subjective quality of the resulting creative outcomes.

Thirty-four undergraduate students, comprising 26 females and 8 males enrolled in a digital textile design course at a South Korean university, participated in the empirical experiment. Prior to the study, all participants had established practical familiarity with standard vector tools in Adobe Illustrator but reported no prior experience with its integrated generative artificial intelligence features. Most participants, representing 85.3 percent of the sample, had interacted with other artificial intelligence tools, primarily ChatGPT, while smaller proportions reported prior exposure to Adobe Firefly or Midjourney. Participants completed projects across five product categories—ball caps, eco-bags, blankets, scarves, and sweatshirts—producing four pattern designs per category under each workflow condition, resulting in twenty completed designs per student. Following task completion, participants completed a comprehensive 50-item survey, and 18 students subsequently engaged in semi-structured qualitative follow-up interviews lasting between 45 and 60 minutes.

To establish a rigorous within-subject comparison, all participants followed a structured sequence wherein they executed their pre-approved conceptual themes using conventional vector-based drawing tools before proceeding to the generative artificial intelligence condition. In the experimental condition, students utilized Firefly-powered text-to-vector generation within Adobe Illustrator, maintaining the option to manually edit and refine the algorithmically generated motifs. Survey instruments evaluated twelve core constructs grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and the Creativity Support Index, capturing intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous procedural load, overall mental workload, and post-task evaluations of creative performance using validated five-point Likert scales.

Quantitative analysis revealed substantial reductions in procedural burden alongside notable constraints on expressive execution. Intrinsic task difficulty dropped significantly under the generative artificial intelligence condition, moving from an average rating of 3.68 out of 5 in the conventional workflow down to 2.09, reflecting a statistically significant decline. Conversely, participants reported that articulating their personal design style became drastically more difficult when using generative tools, dropping from a mean score of 4.24 under the traditional condition to 1.53 in the artificial intelligence condition. This sharp contrast suggests that while automation simplifies structural complexity and eliminates low-level technical friction, it simultaneously restricts the qualitative dimension of intrinsic cognitive processing required to translate an individual stylistic identity into a visual artifact.

Measures of procedural efficiency and editability illustrated a parallel operational trade-off. Participants rated the generative artificial intelligence workflow as significantly more efficient, scoring an average of 4.06 compared to 2.29 for traditional vector tools. However, practical editability ratings were substantially lower for the artificial intelligence condition, scoring 2.47 compared to 3.91 for manual vector methods. Qualitative interview responses illuminated this disparity, with students noting that although generated assets were vector paths in theory, their intricate, machine-generated structures were exceptionally cumbersome to manipulate. Participants frequently observed that correcting unintended geometric errors or altering motif proportions required such exhaustive manual reconstruction that starting a pattern from scratch often felt more efficient than modifying algorithmic outputs.

Ideation patterns further highlighted the nuanced influence of algorithmic assistance on creative divergence. While participants found the process of initiating ideas significantly easier when prompting the model, rating ease of ideation at 3.06 compared to 2.53 in conventional work, the actual quantity of distinct design ideas generated did not demonstrate a statistically significant increase, recording mean scores of 2.97 and 3.44 respectively. Qualitative accounts described this phenomenon as stylistic convergence, wherein the generative engine produced visually appealing yet conceptually uniform variations confined within a narrow aesthetic boundary. Because users lacked fine-grained parameter control, the generative system repeatedly regularized visual features, steering students toward conceptual fixation rather than broad, exploratory design variations.

Overall mental workload decreased dramatically from an average of 4.21 in the conventional setting to 2.15 under algorithmic assistance, yet this reduction did not foster superior design satisfaction. Post-task outcome evaluations revealed that designs produced through manual workflows scored significantly higher across all creative metrics. Perceived creativity and originality fell from 3.94 in conventional work to 2.68 with artificial intelligence assistance. Aesthetic value dropped from 4.09 to 2.74, overall task satisfaction decreased from 3.91 to 2.26, and perceived fulfillment of original design goals plummeted from 4.03 to 2.00. Crucially, measured design engagement showed no statistically significant difference between workflows, indicating that cognitive resources freed by automation were not automatically redirected into deeper conceptual integration or analytical exploration.

Thematic analysis of the qualitative interview data identified four primary experiential dynamics: erosion of creative autonomy, reduced immersion, localized cognitive barriers, and ambivalent assessments of algorithmic utility. Sixteen participants explicitly described feeling that the generative system made executive design choices for them, relegating them to the role of curators rather than active creators.
